title: History and the Ethical Engineer
subtitle: Course Wrap-Up — Can History Help Create a More Just Engineering?

people.name: Eric Schatzberg
people.desc: Course instructor; historian of technology at Georgia Tech; the final week is his synthesis — asking whether historical understanding can help engineers make more just and humane choices.

learn.title: 1 — What Has the Course Argued?
learn.body:
The course's central argument: engineering is not a purely technical practice. It is embedded in social, political, economic, and organizational contexts that shape what gets built, who benefits, who is harmed, and whether safety is maintained. This has been demonstrated in three sections: what engineers do (weeks 1–5), engineering's historical development (weeks 6–10), and ethics case studies (weeks 11–14).

A recurring pattern runs through nearly every case: corporate or political pressure pushes engineers to prioritize cost, speed, and compliance over safety and social welfare. Engineers who resist are sidelined, fired, or — in the Soviet case — killed. The pattern is not new; it did not begin with the 737 Max and will not end there.

learn.title: 2 — What History Teaches Engineers
learn.body: Understanding this history gives engineers three tools. First, pattern recognition: the organizational dynamics in the Pinto case look a lot like the Boeing 737 Max case, which look a lot like the Quebec Bridge case. Recognizing the pattern early — before a disaster — is the goal. Second, moral vocabulary: history provides the ethical concepts (public welfare model, whistleblowing, organizational culture, regulatory capture) needed to articulate what is wrong and why. Third, historical consciousness: current norms are not inevitable — they were made by humans and can be changed.

learn.title: 3 — Can History Help Create a More Just Engineering?
learn.body:
Schatzberg's final question is: can studying history actually help? The pessimistic answer: the pattern keeps repeating despite accumulated knowledge. The Pinto memo happened after Nader; Boeing happened after countless engineering ethics cases were added to curricula. History apparently did not prevent these failures.

The optimistic answer: change is possible and history documents it. The 1966 auto safety law was a real change. Canadian engineering's iron ring is a real cultural intervention. The growth of engineering ethics education, however imperfect, reflects hard-won learning. The answer is not guaranteed progress but: without historical understanding, there is no chance of progress.

learn.title: 4 — Final Exam Preparation
learn.body:
The blue-book final covers weeks 11–15 — Section 3: Ethics of Engineering. Key themes to review: Davis's evolution of engineering ethics codes (Week 11); the Corvair/Pinto cases and cost-benefit analysis vs. consumer safety (Week 12); the Quebec Bridge and organizational culture (Week 13); the 737 Max and managerial revolution / regulatory capture (Week 14); and Week 15's synthesis.

The exam tests your ability to analyze cases using the course's conceptual tools — not just recall facts. Be prepared to identify the ethical failures in a case, explain what institutional factors enabled them, and connect them to broader course themes. Practice writing clear, argued essays in the blue book — handwriting counts.

anki.q: What is the course's central argument about engineering?
anki.a: Engineering is not purely technical — it is embedded in social, political, economic, and organizational contexts that shape what gets built, who benefits, who is harmed, and whether safety is maintained.

anki.q: What 'recurring pattern' does the course identify across engineering history?
anki.a: Corporate or political pressure pushes engineers to prioritize cost, speed, and compliance over safety and social welfare — from the copper-cooled engine to the Pinto to the 737 Max.

anki.q: What three tools does historical understanding give engineers?
anki.a: Pattern recognition (recognize the organizational dynamics before disaster); moral vocabulary (ethical concepts to articulate failures); historical consciousness (current norms were made by humans and can change).

anki.q: What is 'historical consciousness' and why does it matter for engineers?
anki.a: Awareness that present institutions, technologies, and norms are historically contingent — they were made by humans and can be changed by humans. Essential for imagining and advocating for change.

anki.q: What is the pessimistic answer to whether history can help create better engineering?
anki.a: The pattern keeps repeating despite accumulated knowledge — the Pinto memo happened after Nader; Boeing happened after countless ethics cases were added to curricula. History apparently doesn't prevent failures.

anki.q: What is the optimistic answer to whether history can help create better engineering?
anki.a: Change is possible and history documents it — the 1966 auto safety law was real change; the iron ring is a real cultural intervention. Without historical understanding there is no chance of progress.

anki.q: How does Riley's Week 1 argument connect to the course's final lesson?
anki.a: The course's entire arc demonstrates Riley's argument empirically — engineering cultures that suppress social and ethical awareness produce disasters; awareness of this history supports her call for social justice engineering.

anki.q: What weeks does the final blue-book exam cover?
When and where is the final exam?
anki.a: Tuesday, December 15, 2026, 2:40–5:30 PM — blue-book format in the scheduled exam room.

anki.q: What does 'pattern recognition' give engineers who study history?
anki.a: The ability to recognize organizational dynamics that precede engineering disasters — seeing the copper-cooled, Pinto, and 737 Max pattern early enough to intervene, before people die.

anki.q: What is the 'recurring pattern of failure' the course has traced?
anki.a: Corporate/political pressure + organizational culture that silences concerns + uncritical problem-solving = preventable engineering disasters. This pattern recurs from the 1920s copper-cooled engine to the 2018 737 Max.

anki.q: How should students approach the blue-book final exam?
anki.a: Analyze cases using the course's conceptual tools (ethics models, organizational culture, regulatory capture, etc.) — not just recall facts. Write clear, argued essays. Handwriting counts.

anki.q: What is 'moral vocabulary' as the course develops it?
anki.a: The ethical concepts — public welfare model, whistleblowing, organizational culture, regulatory capture — that let engineers articulate precisely what is wrong in a failure case and why.

anki.q: What does the iron ring (Canada) represent as a course conclusion?
anki.a: That engineering cultures can consciously embed historical awareness of failure into professional identity — turning a disaster into a permanent, physical reminder of professional responsibility.

anki.q: What would Palchinsky (Week 10) say about the 737 Max?
anki.a: He would recognize the pattern: engineering knowledge suppressed by organizational pressure, warnings ignored, human costs treated as acceptable losses. His principles — consider human costs, design for learning — were violated throughout.

quiz.q: What is the course's central recurring pattern across all engineering failure cases?
options: Engineers lack sufficient technical training
Corporate or political pressure consistently pushes engineers to prioritize cost and speed over safety — from the copper-cooled engine to the 737 Max
Regulators are always at fault when engineering fails
Engineering disasters only happen when engineers are dishonest
quiz.explanation: The pattern recurs across cases and eras: organizational pressure silences engineering judgment, safety is subordinated to financial or political priorities, and people die preventably.

quiz.q: What does 'historical consciousness' give engineers that purely technical training does not?
options: Better calculation skills
Awareness that current norms were made by humans and can be changed — essential for recognizing and resisting recurring failure patterns
Knowledge of historical bridge designs
The ability to predict future disasters with certainty
quiz.explanation: Historical consciousness — understanding that present conditions are contingent, not inevitable — allows engineers to imagine and advocate for different professional cultures and institutional arrangements.

quiz.q: What is the pessimistic reading of whether history education prevents engineering disasters?
options: History education is too expensive
The pattern keeps repeating despite accumulated knowledge — Pinto happened after Nader; Boeing happened after decades of ethics education
Students don't take history courses
Historical cases are too old to be relevant
quiz.explanation: The pessimist notes that knowing about the Pinto case didn't stop Boeing — suggesting that history education alone is insufficient without structural change.

quiz.q: The final blue-book exam covers which section of the course?
options: Weeks 1–5 (What Engineers Do)
Weeks 6–10 (Engineering in the 19th and 20th Centuries)
Weeks 11–15 (Ethics of Engineering)
The entire course
quiz.explanation: The final exam covers weeks 11–15 — Section 3: Ethics of Engineering, including Davis's codes, the Corvair/Pinto, Quebec Bridge, Boeing 737 Max, and the wrap-up.

quiz.q: What connecting thread links Riley's Week 1 argument to the Week 15 course conclusion?
options: Both focus exclusively on the 737 Max
The entire course demonstrates Riley's argument empirically — engineering cultures that suppress ethical awareness produce disasters; history supports her call for social justice engineering
Riley and Schatzberg disagree on the main causes of engineering failure
Week 15 abandons Riley's argument as too idealistic
quiz.explanation: Riley's opening argument — that the problem-solving mindset without ethical awareness is dangerous — is proven empirically by every case in the course. The conclusion circles back to her challenge.
